explanation: Control flow, the order in which instructions are executed, is fundamental to program behavior.  In computer architecture, control flow is implemented using conditional jumps and branches based on the results of comparisons or other conditions. Understanding how high-level language constructs translate into assembly instructions that manipulate control flow is crucial for optimizing performance and understanding low-level system behavior.

extraction_metadata.source: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (3rd Edition)

book: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (3rd Edition)
code_example:
; High-Level IF implemented using Jumps
CMP RDI, 10       ; RDI - 10, sets flags (ZF, CF, SF)
JGE  END_IF       ; Jump if Greater or Equal (False path)

; IF block executes if RDI < 10
MOV RAX, 100
JMP  CONTINUE

END_IF:
; ELSE block (or code after IF skipped)
MOV RAX, 0

CONTINUE:


; WHILE Loop Structure
LOOP_START:
CMP  RCX, 0       ; Test loop counter
JE   LOOP_EXIT    ; Jump if Equal (RCX == 0)

; Loop Body
DEC  RCX          ; Decrement counter
JMP  LOOP_START

LOOP_EXIT:
; Loop finished
keywords: Conditional Jumps, Assembly Control Flow, CPU Branching, Status Flags
